statements: The chief concern is a several-year history of slowly progressive purple spots on both feet.
The purple spots increased in number and size.
Clinically, the lesions are multiple purple papules and plaques on the dorsum of the feet and around the ankles.
Some of the lesions are crusted.
In an older man, bilateral violaceous acral lesions raise concern for a vascular proliferation.
Kaposi sarcoma is a particular concern in this setting.
The diagnosis must be reconciled with the biopsy.
Salient positive findings include chronic, gradual enlargement over years.
Salient positive findings include bilateral acral distribution on the feet and ankles.
Salient positive findings include violaceous papules and plaques.
Histology shows a vascular lesion extending from the papillary dermis to the reticular dermis in a lobular pattern.
The lesion is composed mainly of dilated blood-filled thin-walled spaces.
The lesion also contains some thick-walled vessels.
Histology shows hemosiderin deposition.
Histology shows chronic inflammation.
Histology shows focal immature vascular clefts with extravasated erythrocytes.
Histology shows mild endothelial atypia.
These features indicate a benign-to-borderline vascular proliferation with hemorrhagic change.
There are no systemic symptoms.
There is no lymphadenopathy.
There is no visceral involvement.
HIV serology is negative.
There is no spindle cell proliferation on histology.
The absence of spindle cell proliferation argues strongly against Kaposi sarcoma despite the clinical resemblance.
There is no mention of dissecting irregular anastomosing vascular channels infiltrating collagen.
There is no mention of marked atypia.
There is no mention of multilayered endothelium.
These missing features do not support angiosarcoma.
The lesion is not described as a simple targetoid solitary papule typical of hobnail hemangioma.
Histology instead shows larger dilated vessels with hemosiderin and focal papillary-dermal slitlike immature areas.
There is no systemic disease to support epidemic Kaposi sarcoma.
There is no immunosuppression to support iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.
The leading differential is acroangiodermatitis.
Acroangiodermatitis is also called pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma.
The leading differential is particularly the Mali type or a related acral reactive vascular proliferation.
Acroangiodermatitis fits the bilateral lesions on the feet and ankles of an older man.
Acroangiodermatitis fits the histology of capillary and venous proliferation with thick- and thin-walled vessels, hemosiderin, extravasated erythrocytes, and inflammation.
Acroangiodermatitis can clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma.
Acroangiodermatitis may show vascular clefts and mild endothelial atypia.
Acroangiodermatitis lacks the spindle-cell fascicles characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is the main competing diagnosis.
Kaposi sarcoma is considered because of the violaceous plaques on the feet.
Kaposi sarcoma is considered because of the focal slitlike vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes.
Kaposi sarcoma is less likely because HIV serology is negative.
Kaposi sarcoma is less likely because there is no systemic involvement.
Kaposi sarcoma is less likely because the biopsy lacks spindle cell proliferation.
Spindle cell proliferation is a key histologic feature of Kaposi sarcoma.
Another consideration is verrucous hemangioma or another benign venous or lymphatic vascular malformation.
This consideration is based on the hyperkeratotic epidermis and dilated vascular spaces.
The age of onset is in late adulthood.
The lesions have a bilateral multifocal acral distribution.
The lesions have a pseudo-Kaposi-like clinical appearance.
These features make verrucous hemangioma or another benign venous or lymphatic vascular malformation less fitting.
Angiosarcoma is low likelihood.
Angiosarcoma is low likelihood because the course is indolent over years.
Angiosarcoma is low likelihood because histology shows only mild atypia without destructive infiltrative malignant features.

The combination of bilateral slowly progressive violaceous acral plaques, absence of systemic disease, and biopsy showing lobular dilated vascular proliferation with hemosiderin and extravasated erythrocytes but no spindle cell proliferation most strongly supports acroangiodermatitis.
Acroangiodermatitis is the final diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis includes acroangiodermatitis with high likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes Kaposi sarcoma with medium likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes angiosarcoma with low likelihood.
The final diagnosis is acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma).

clusters.label: history_taking
clusters.summary: Chronic progressive bilateral purple spots on the feet enlarged over years.

clusters.label: examination
clusters.summary: Physical exam describes bilateral violaceous papules and plaques on the feet and ankles, some crusted.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Clinical concern is raised for a vascular proliferation, especially Kaposi sarcoma, based on the acral violaceous lesions and chronic course.

clusters.label: examination
clusters.summary: Biopsy shows a lobular vascular proliferation with dilated blood-filled spaces, hemosiderin, inflammation, slitlike areas, and mild atypia, suggesting a benign-to-borderline hemorrhagic vascular lesion.

clusters.label: other
clusters.summary: No systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, visceral involvement, or HIV infection are present.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, and hobnail hemangioma are argued against by the absence of spindle cells, marked atypia, infiltrative features, and supportive systemic context.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Acroangiodermatitis is proposed as the leading diagnosis, fitting the acral bilateral lesions and reactive vascular histology while lacking Kaposi-type spindle-cell fascicles.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Kaposi sarcoma remains the main competing diagnosis but is downgraded by negative HIV, no systemic disease, and absent spindle-cell proliferation.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Verrucous hemangioma or another benign vascular malformation is considered but fits poorly with the late-onset bilateral pseudo-Kaposi-like presentation.

clusters.label: differential_generation
clusters.summary: Angiosarcoma is considered unlikely because the course is indolent and histology lacks destructive malignant atypia.

clusters.label: final_decision
clusters.summary: The overall clinicopathologic picture most strongly supports acroangiodermatitis, which is stated as the final diagnosis.
